title: Knight of TWO Hearts
author: Marcus
synopsis: Subtitle: A valley starves while a king blames a dragon and the river turns foul. Young knight Roblen climbs to a mountain cave to kill a beast and finds a guardian instead. Nathan lies weakened by poisoned water. In the chamber beyond, a stone vault bears the record of an old oath. A ruler once shared half a heart with the keeper of the valley, and prosperity followed truth. Roblen places his palm upon the cut and chooses to bind his life to the guardian. With healer Serenya, scholar Ceyrin, river man Garran, and captain Sir Kaelor, he follows

chapters.title: About the Author
chapters.content:
About the Author

I am a writer who loves to follow my imagination wherever it leads. One day I might create a mystery thriller, another day a touching love story, or even a wild adventure with space battles and dragons hidden in lost worlds.

Stories have always been a way to escape, to dream, and to face challenges with courage. Writing became the place where imagination could run free, sometimes into a mystery thriller, sometimes into a tender love story, and other times into adventures with dragons or distant galaxies.

The journey began in school and was carried quietly for years until the moment came to finally share it. Now those worlds are open for anyone who wishes to step inside, explore, and find something worth remembering long after the last page.

To discover more books and new adventures, visit www.marekpuchon.com

chapters.title: Hunger in the Land
chapters.content:
Hunger in the Land

Snow did not fall that winter. A pale sky held itself like a cracked bowl over the valley, and the wind came dry from the mountains. Fields that should have slept under a white quilt lay open and hard as old bone. Stubble rasped beneath boots, and frost clung to the broken stalks as if afraid to melt. Crows gathered on fence rails and pecked at nothing, patient and mean. Dogs no longer barked at them. Dogs had grown quiet.

The smell of smoke drifted over the king’s road. Not the warm kind from hearths. Bitter smoke from wet wood, from empty kitchens where a pot boiled only to darken water and trick the eye. At the mile stone that marked the boundary of the royal demesne, a woman held a clay bowl under a frozen well rope and waited, as if patience alone could pull water from rock. Roblen set his pack down, braced for the weight, and worked the crank for her. The rope groaned. A rush of air rose from the shaft, dry and hollow. No water answered.

“Thank you,” she said. The voice carried a worn thread of courtesy that refused to break. A child stood behind her with lips cracked white and eyes too large for his face.

“Is there a stream near?” Roblen asked.

“South of the willow cut,” she said. “It tastes like coins.”

The boy nodded, then looked at Roblen’s sword, and the way his hand rested near the hilt. That look had become common along the road. People had begun to weigh the shape of a blade the way they once weighed bread.

Roblen reached into his pack and drew out a wrapped heel. He had divided his rations before leaving the barracks. None of it would save a village, yet a gift could anchor a morning. He broke the bread, gave the larger piece to the boy, and the smaller to the woman. Both whispered a blessing without meeting his eyes. Shame rose and fell, like a cough he could not clear. He thanked them for the blessing and went on.

The west road rose to a ridge, then ran along a line of coppiced beech and oak. From there the land opened. He saw the river coil in the distance, a dark thread through the dull fields. On its near bank, the royal town huddled in a ring of pale stone. Towers lifted above smoke and winter haze, watchful and spare. Banners hung at half mast, their cloth thin with age, their colors bruised. The crown had ordered the flags lowered until the famine broke. A sign of sorrow. A sign of power. To many it had become a reminder.

Roblen slowed as the road entered the outer market. Stalls leaned like tired men, their awnings patched and sagging. The spicers had shuttered their boards. The fish sellers stood on bare planks as if guarding an idea rather than a trade. A potter had stacked thirty bowls on a blanket, and not one bore a mark. The glaze had cracked in a pattern like spider silk, pretty and useless. She smiled anyway, and talc dusted her hairline where a hat should have been.

“You look like a man who takes care of his cups,” she said. It was a brave joke. He smiled back and bought a small bowl for more than its worth. The coin made a dull sound on the blanket. She wrapped the bowl in a strip of worn linen and thanked him three times.

When he moved on, a whisper followed. Dragon. Some spat the word. Some breathed it, an old fear made new. Men at the meat hooks, with nothing to hang there, leaned close and said the name the court criers shouted. Nacreban Iske Nordin. A mouthful of the old tongue. It tasted like stone and smoke when spoken aloud. Few used it. Most said simply the beast.

At the square, the king’s herald stood on a plank stage and beat a drum. The sound reached only the first ring of people. Those farther out watched the drumstick rise and fall and guessed the words. A parchment hung from the herald’s hand, ribboned and sealed.

“Hear the sorrow of Halric, your king,” the herald cried. “Hear the truth that chokes our fields. The dragon that lairs in the mountain has fouled our rivers, with breath, with will, with old hate. The creature drinks and the land thirsts. By the mercy of the crown, a champion will rise, strike the monster, and break the curse. By the mercy of the crown, the granaries will open when the beast lies dead.”

A murmur spread, a ripple through dry grass. Some cheered. Others crossed themselves and studied their feet. One man laughed once, loud and quick, then pressed a hand over his mouth and turned away.

Roblen did not cheer. The words had weight, yet the shape of them leaned wrong. A child does not crush a wheat sheaf, yet a child can tell when a cart tilts. He looked up at the high balcony above the square. Stiff figures lined it, cloaks cinched to the throat, hands hidden in warm sleeves. King Halric stood at the center, a crown on his head, his jaw set in a straight, hard line. To the king’s right, Sir Kaelor wore polished mail that caught what little light the sun offered. Kaelor’s eyes swept the crowd without interest, then fell to the stage. A nod sent the herald on.

“By command of the crown,” the herald said, “the king calls for a knight with a true heart to ride against the dragon. Let this name be spoken.” He looked down at the parchment, then lifted his chin. “Roblen of the lower ward.”

The square paused, as if a sigh had grown too large to release. A few heads turned toward him with slow recognition. He stepped forward. Boots made a hollow sound on the planks. The world seemed to narrow, like a long corridor built of faces. He climbed the steps and faced the herald, then the balcony. Wind tugged at his cloak and found the sweat at his neck.

King Halric raised a hand. The motion was practiced, and it held the quiet a little too long. “Roblen,” the king said, voice carrying in that trained way rulers learn. “Your record names courage. Your superiors speak of steadiness. I ask service, and I promise reward.”

“Majesty,” Roblen said. He bowed, not too deep. “I am yours to command.”

The king’s eyes remained cool and small in the pale winter light. “Ride to the mountain. Find the lair. Slay the dragon. Bring me the head, and I will open the gates of the granary. Fail, and the land fails with you.”

It was a cruel shape, dressed in ceremony. The crown placed a weight upon one man and called it mercy. Roblen felt it settle across his shoulders, real as mail. He opened his mouth to answer and closed it again. Words could bruise a moment. Care made them fit better.

“I will ride,” he said. The voice came out low and even. The people needed even more than they needed loud.

A stir moved through the crowd. A woman near the stage began to cry in that private way that continues even when a hand covers the mouth. A boy raised both fists and shook them at the balcony, a small fury with no plan. His father pulled the fists down and held them close to the boy’s chest until the shaking eased.

Sir Kaelor left the balcony and crossed the square with a measured pace, as if the distance itself had to be reminded who stepped upon it. He climbed the stage, saluted the herald, then faced Roblen. Close to, the older knight’s hair showed iron among the black, and his eyes had the color of river stones in shade.

“Come,” Kaelor said. “The armory waits.”

They left the stage together. The crowd opened like a tired door and closed again behind them. Roblen kept his hands loose at his sides. The habit of resting near the hilt is meant to warn fools. In a hungry city it can warn friends.

Within the keep, the air warmed and thickened. Beeswax and old oak. Smoke in the banners. A long table held maps with edges gone soft from years of fingers and decisions. Kaelor led him through, to a narrow stair, then down to the armory. The keeper of arms stood by a stand of spears and shook his head as if it might clear dust from thought. He bowed to Kaelor, nodded to Roblen, and laid out choices.

“Mail shirt,” Kaelor said. “Good rings, no slack. You will need freedom of shoulder. The creature flies.” He considered a moment. “Take a heater shield. A kite shield drags in wind. The mountain has wind.”

Roblen drew on the mail. Links whispered over linen. The weight felt right. He strapped the shield, then took the sword he favored. Not the court blade with jeweled cross. The one he had used in the practice yard for years, with a grip worn smooth by work. Kaelor saw the choice and said nothing, which was approval in his dialect.

“Listen,” Kaelor said. He stood near, and the voice lost some of its court brass. “You will ride alone, as the king commanded. We will watch the road, and we will hold the city. That is the order. Do not mistake the king’s patience for softness. Bring back what is asked.”

“What if the beast does not cause the blight,” Roblen asked. It was not the bold question it sounded like. It was a simple request for the story to fit the shape of the world.

Kaelor’s jaw worked once, then eased. “I trust the crown,” he said. “I trust the need.” The pause that followed came uninvited. “I trust you to do your best for those who cannot lift a sword.” He touched two fingers to the badge stitched at Roblen’s shoulder. “Carry that well.”

Outside, the afternoon leaned toward evening. A gray gold light fell over the stones and turned them older than they had looked at noon. Roblen crossed the lower ward, where wash lines hung without wash, and the smell of cabbage water drifted from open doors. A girl drew a shape in soot on a wall, three lines that met and crossed. Some called it a warding sign. Others called it just something to do.

Near the south gate, a narrow house bore a white mark above the lintel. The healer’s mark, hand painted, careful and clean. Roblen paused and knocked. A voice called from within, warm and steady. Lady Serenya opened the door with a cup of tea in one hand and a cloth in the other. Hair the color of dark wheat lay braided over one shoulder. The room behind her smelled of thyme and clean wood.

“You walk like a man sent to do a thing he already regrets,” she said. It came out gentle, not sharp.

“You always begin with comfort,” Roblen said. “Then you press.”

“Sit,” she said. She set the cup on the table and drew the cloth through careful fingers. “Drink before you try to carry courage. It rides better after tea.”

He sat. The chair creaked with a friendly honesty that made him smile despite himself. The tea could have been grass steeped in warm water, yet it held a kindness. He drank, and the warmth found the cold place at the center of his chest and loosened it.

“The king has named the cause, has he,” Serenya said. She did not give the name. Some avoided it, as if the syllables themselves might open a door.

“He has,” Roblen answered.

“And he has named the cure.”

“A blade.”

Serenya watched the steam roll from the cup. “A river does not sour from dragon breath,” she said. “I have treated bellies that twist and throats that parch, and the pattern runs wrong for old tales. Fish brought to me from the lower bend carry a thin sheen that smells of pitch. It is not magic. It is muck.”

“From where,” he asked.

“I am a healer, not a lord of lands,” she said. “I know only this. The river brings what someone gives it. That which it gives now is harm.” She met his eyes. “You will ride anyway.”

“I will ride,” he said. Duty named the path. Doubt walked beside it. Both had voices. Both could be true.

“Then ride with your eyes open,” she said. “And keep your heart open a little as well. A closed heart cuts its own bearer first.”

He finished the tea and stood. “You will be safe,” he said. It was a habit to ask without asking.

“As safe as any,” she said. “Safer than those who must pass the south bend for water.” The cloth in her hands stilled. “If you find truth, bring it back, not only a trophy.”

“I will try,” he said.

Night gathered while he checked his gear in the stable. The mare watched him with the slow patience of good animals that know a man’s weight and forgive it. Roblen brushed her coat until it shone like sealed leather, then fed an apple and saved another in the saddlebag. He tightened girth and counted straps by touch. A small habit, old as his first days under arms, and never set aside.

When the moon lifted over the inner wall, he rode to the gate. Torches hissed in their sconces, spitting a little rain left from a short, mean cloud. The gatekeeper yawned into his shoulder, then straightened when he saw the badge and the mail.

“Open for Sir Roblen,” the guard said. The title sat odd in the mouth, too formal for a man who had earned his place with work rather than ceremony. The chains rattled, the portcullis rose, and the cold beyond breathed its hard breath into the arch.

Roblen looked back once. Windows in the lower ward glowed, here and there. The glow had a quality he had learned to read. Families saved oil in hunger, and so the light that remained became precious and slow. It marked rooms where people chose to sit near each other rather than sleep early and ration dreams. He lifted a hand. No one saw it. The gesture was for him.

Beyond the wall, the road fell into quiet. Hoofbeats rolled ahead in a hollow drum, then faded into the bare trees and low frost. Far off, an owl gave three calls, not quite even. The pattern tugged at memory. An old children’s rhyme answered in his head without permission. Three beats for warning, two for safe, one for home. He smiled at the foolish comfort.

The river came into view near the second willow cut. Not a silver thing. A dark band that held light only where it broke on stones. He dismounted and led the mare to the edge. The water lapped with a small, tired sound. When he filled his palm the surface held a dull skin that slid and stretched before it tore. He lifted it to his nose. Coins, as the woman had said. Coins and tar. He spat and rinsed his mouth in clean snow. The mare snorted and turned her head away from the water.

Upstream, a glow marked the old mill. Wheels stood still. No one wasted force in winter when there was no grain to grind. Yet a faint light burned within. He led the mare to the door and knocked. It opened at once, as if the hand had hovered there waiting.

An old man stood with a lantern. Lines around the mouth drew down so deep they looked carved. He lifted the light and studied Roblen’s mail, then the sword, then the eyes.

“Traveling late,” the man said.

“Rising early,” Roblen said.

The man made a sound that could have been a laugh if laughter had bones to scrape. “You have the look of a rider sent to the mountain.”

Roblen did not deny it. “I have questions about the river.”

“You and everyone,” the man said. He turned and waved Roblen in. The mill smelled of damp grain and old work. Sacks lay flat along the wall like tired men asleep on their sides. “I draw water up here for my wife’s washing,” the man said. “It makes the cloth smell like the shipyard. We never had a shipyard.”

“Have you seen men at the banks,” Roblen asked. “Barrels, carts, anything that does not belong.”

“Not by day,” the man said. “Night carries a sound sometimes. A slap of oar. A whisper of men who do not wish to be men in daylight. I sleep light and rather than chase shadows, I bank the fire.”

Roblen listened to the river outside. It kept its counsel. He thanked the man and turned to go.

“Sir,” the old miller said, and the word did not flatter. It simply named a soul who had taken on a weight. “If you find that beast and it proves a beast, give it the clean end of your blade. If you find something else, do not mistake killing for cure.”

“I will remember,” Roblen said.

He rode on until the town lay behind a screen of hill and thicket. The road narrowed and the moon climbed a little higher and lost some of its size. He thought of the square, of the herald’s drum, and of the king’s eyes when he spoke the word reward. He thought of Serenya’s calm and the taste of coin on the water. He pictured the mountain that hung over every child’s drawing of home, that black tooth on the edge of the world.

At a bend where three birches leaned together, he drew rein and swung down. The ground offered a shelf of dry leaves under a low spruce. He set a small fire in a chimney of stones and kept it mean, the way soldiers keep a flame that warms hands without telling a stranger its story. The mare cropped at brown grass and pretended to be content. He ate with simple care, then wrapped his cloak tight and settled with his back to the tree.

Sleep came in pieces, stitched by the sound of the river and the soft clink of the mare’s bit. Between those pieces, thoughts rose and fell. A river soured by a breath that had never touched it. A king who offered mercy with the weight of iron. A people who wanted a head on a spike and bread on a plate and did not much care which came first if only something came.

Before dawn, the fire had become a friendly bruise in the stones. The sky held a slow gray that promised nothing and delivered that promise well. Roblen stood and brushed leaf dust from his mail. He touched the mare’s neck, then set his boot in the stirrup.

“Come on then,” he said to the cold air, to the road, to whatever waited beyond the next line of trees. “Let us see what truth the mountain guards.”

The mare answered with a small stamp that sent frost from the grass in a silver drift. He turned her nose toward the north and rode. The land rose in long swells. The wind shaped itself into a keener tone. Far ahead, the mountain lifted its shoulder against the sky, dark and patient. Somewhere within that stone, a lair waited. Somewhere above the lair, smoke would rise, or it would not. The only way to know was forward.

He did not pray. Not as some prayed, with words and bargains. He kept his breath steady and his eyes open and let the rhythm of hoof and heart make its own kind of asking. The kingdom lay behind him and before him both, hungry and watchful, ready to name a monster and ready to be saved. He would bring back what the road gave, and he would make sure it was the truth and not only a trophy. The promise sat in his chest like a coal that refused to cool.

The birches thinned, and the last hedgerow gave out. The mountain’s shadow reached across the road and covered him like a cloak. He did not shiver. He set his jaw, and he rode on.

chapters.title: A Knight’s Burden
chapters.content:
A Knight’s Burden

Morning rose with a color that could not decide itself. Not gold, not gray, something between that made the world hold its breath. Frost toed the path in a thin line. Each hoof print pressed a small flower into that pale skin, then let the bloom fade. Roblen kept the mare to an easy walk until warmth found the legs and the saddle settled into the day. Sparse trees stood like careful men along the verge. Branches held a rim of ice that cracked when a rook landed and shook the limb.

Silence on the road did not feel empty. It held weight. The kind that comes when a promise has been made and cannot be called back. Roblen kept his gaze moving. Fence rails lean, gate latches broken, roof thatch pulled and patched with reed and hope. Life still held on, but with short nails.

A mile past the last hedgerow, a stone shrine stood where the road bent. Nothing grand. Two pillars and a lintel, all weathered, all plain. The time worn figure within had lost half a face to years and winter. Someone had set a little clay dish at the base and lined it with dried berries. A poor gift but a true one. Roblen dismounted, tied the mare to a low branch, and stepped under the lintel. Cold gathered there in a still pocket. He put down a coin and touched the stone with his knuckles in the old way. No words. The silence knew the shape of his ask.

When he turned back he saw a girl on the road, a basket looped over one arm, a length of cord tied to her wrist. The cord ran to a goat with ribs like a ladder. Both watched him with the same measure of caution, the sort that keeps a soul from losing what little still belongs to it.

“Good morning,” Roblen said.

“Good if you ate,” the girl answered. Her voice had more muscle than her arms.

He offered the apple from his saddlebag. The goat smelled it and pulled so hard the cord creaked. The girl laughed once and eased the apple from his hand with care, as if kindness might crack if held wrong. She cut the fruit in three with a small knife. One piece to the goat. One to Roblen. One for herself. The goat finished first and looked aggrieved that the world had only one apple in it.

“Where does the road go,” she asked. “For you, I mean.”

“The mountain,” Roblen said.

She looked at his sword. “For the dragon then.”

“For what waits there,” he said. It was as honest as he could make a sentence and still let it stand upright.

“My mother says the river makes her hands itch,” the girl said. “She washes anyway. A person can only carry so much snow from the woods.” A short shrug, more from habit than belief. “When you get to the mountain, ask it to stop making the water bad.”

“I will ask,” he said. He meant it, though the mountain would likely answer in stone and wind rather than words.

They walked together for a short stretch, the goat giving the road a look of insult each time a pebble offended a hoof. At a fork the girl pointed left with two fingers.

“Path to the ferryman,” she said. “Straight on for the old quarry. Both take you to the big bend. The bend smells worst.”

“Thank you,” Roblen said. “Keep your apple knife sharp.”

“I keep everything sharp,” she said, then tugged the goat and turned down the left way with a little lift to her walk, as if three bites of sweetness still talked to her legs.

Roblen chose the straight road. The quarry rose after a while, a broken tooth in the low hills. Stone blocks lay where men had left them when wheat once grew tall. A cart wheel leaned on a wall. Spokes gone. Hub wedged with straw. He led the mare across a bridge of granite slabs placed long ago by hands that had known how to make weight behave. The river called from far below with a voice that had not slept in a long time and did not plan to.

At the crest of the next rise the world opened. The valley floor showed its ribs. Winter grass bowed to a wind that ran in narrow lanes. Far off, a clutch of houses clung to a point where the river bent and foamed. A black line of pines flanked the slope beyond. Above all, the mountain sat with its back to the sky, a great shoulder of dark stone cut with scars of snow.

Roblen took in the sight and let it settle. Sights like that can fill a man if he lets them. Pride if he is foolish. Right kind of humility if he is not. He urged the mare on. The sun struggled above a cloud like a child crawling onto a wall to see a parade. The day would not warm much.

Before noon, smoke carried a faint smell of fish and willow twig. The cluster of houses at the bend had been built where the river pinched itself and made a quick, shallow run. Poles stood along the bank with nets drooping like weary flags. Men knelt by a skiff and scraped at the boards with flint shards. Women rolled wet cloth over wooden staves and struck it with smooth paddles, faces turned away from spray that did not taste right.

Roblen reined in at the edge of the little green. A figure came out from a door that did not fit its frame and tugged it shut behind him with a mumble of oath. Thick arms. Thick neck. A face that had once known laughter as a daily trade and had put that trade aside during hard years. The man wiped hands on his coat and stopped a few paces away, careful enough to give space without ceding ground.

“You carry the city on your shoulders,” the man said. “Or the city put a weight on you. Either way it shows.”

“I carry a task,” Roblen said. “And questions where water runs thin.”

“You and everyone,” the man said, echo of the miller without knowing it. He nodded to a girl who stood in her doorway and watched with the same private stare that children practice when the world makes speeches. “Ask then. Fair trade if answer bought a loaf.”

“What rides this river besides water,” Roblen asked. “By night.”

The man rubbed the side of his nose with thumb and thought a moment. “Three weeks back, a boat came through late,” he said. “No lantern. No oars singing. Only a scuff like a hand that did not want to be heard. We keep a night fire on the bend. My nephew tossed a stick to feed it and the light climbed the bank just right to see what knew it should not be seen. Two men in dark coats. A third crouched by the side and poured from a small barrel. Not a fisher barrel. Narrow and tall like a priest. When the barrel emptied he swung it twice and let the river take it. No words spoken. Work done tidy. Boat went on.”

“Faces,” Roblen asked.

“Faces do not like to be looked at during that sort of chore,” the man said. “But I remember the way one set his feet. In the manner of a soldier who wishes to pretend he has not been trained. Hard to hide the way a leg holds a knee. Habit tells on a man.”

“Did you send word,” Roblen asked.

“We sent a boy to the old mill,” the man said. “The old man there has ears that tell him more than most. I do not know if the word walked beyond that. River folk keep tales close. The city listens when it wishes and the crown answers when it must. Lately it has not wished and it has not musted.” He shrugged, apology and anger both. “I have a boat. I cannot fight men who throw barrels in the dark and claim the sky did it.”

Roblen looked at the water and saw the sheen again, thin, almost beautiful if a person did not know what it did to bellies and throats. He crouched and dipped a bowl, not to drink, but to let the light make a skin. The bowl bore a small flaw where the glaze had bubbled. It would suit for more than soup. He poured the water out and tucked the bowl back safe.

“I will ride upriver,” he said. “If men do what you say, they will have left prints on bank mud or drag marks on stone. Not much rain since last week. A track can last.”

The man nodded. “We mend nets,” he said. “We mend boats. I do not know how to mend a river. If you find a way, mend it swift.” He set his hands on his hips and leaned into a stretch that popped his back. “My name is Garran. If you return and still breathe, come through and eat what can be spared.”

“Roblen,” he said. “I will return if I am able.” He took a breath that tasted of ash and bad fish and lifted into the saddle.

The bank narrowed beyond the bend. Willow roots reached like gnarled fingers into the current. A thin path ran above the water where boys would have run in better seasons. He rode with care. Twice he dismounted and led the mare around a fallen trunk. Twice more he pushed brush back with the flat of his blade while it left brown streaks on the steel and a wet smell on his gloves.

Signs showed where men had already passed. One line of prints that did not belong to the village. Boots that had come from money. Even heel. Tight stitch on the side. Not the split raw kind that comes from hard years and wet work. Drag marks cut the mud where something narrow had been pulled from a boat to the bank. A shoulder had carried the weight in a smart way. Leave no deep hole where a foot settles. Spread weight. Use the bank grass to clean a boot on the way out. Care that reveals a mind.

Roblen knelt and touched a print. Cold came through the glove and into the bones of his fingers. The man who had made it had set the foot with calm. No rush. Work familiar. He stood and followed the line to where the path climbed a short bluff and flattened under a stand of alder. There the trail broke. Men had scattered needles to make a clean carpet and walked over it in mixed steps. Harder to read when the ground had been set to confuse. He smiled despite himself. It was a good trick. Old tricks can still make a hand respect the player.

The day leaned past noon without losing any light. It had not offered much to begin with. Wind stiffened and found spots in his mail where winter could bite the skin. He let the mare rest under a pine and chewed a strip of dried meat that wanted to be called a meal. The river kept talking. The sound changed a little where stones bit deeper or where a deeper run opened. He listened and let the water tell what it would. At times listening is the only weapon that will fit the hand.

In mid afternoon a patrol of three rode down from the ridge. Livery of the crown hung clean on their coats. Faces held that watchful blank that says a man knows you from training and not from story. The lead rider lifted two fingers in a curt hail and drew up, careful to keep distance polite.

“Sir Roblen,” the rider said. “By order of the crown, we carry notice.”

“Speak it,” Roblen said. He kept his own hands still and open on the reins.

“King Halric reminds all who serve,” the rider recited, “that the cause of blight is the dragon in the mountain. All men are to give aid to the chosen knight who rides there. All others are to clear the road and keep watch on the river. If enemies of the crown disturb water or land, seize them and hold for judgment.”

Roblen looked at the man, then at the paper rolled and sealed in his hand. “Have you seen enemies of the crown on this stretch,” he asked.

“We have seen hunger,” the rider said. “Hunger does not wear colors.” A tight half smile showed and went away. “We change watch at the fork above the quarry. If you need a fresh mount, ask. Orders say to assist.”

“I will keep to my own mare,” Roblen said.

“Then ride with a straight eye,” the rider said. “Road ends at stone soon enough.” He nodded, wheeled, and led his men up the path. Hooves picked at rock in a rhythm that said the horses trusted their riders and their riders trusted the day only as far as a man should.

The river made a last clean run through shelves of black slate, then narrowed into a cut. Walls of stone rose and stole the view of all but a ribbon of sky. Sound grew loud and close. The mare laid ears back and moved in quick, careful steps. Roblen felt the space fold around them and breathed shallow to make his chest small. At the far end of the cut, the world opened again to a bowl of valley that lay right under the mountain. Snow clung to shadows. Dark grass pushed through where sun touched. A ring of old stones lifted from the ground like teeth around a broken jaw. People had once met there to speak to someone who answered from wind and cloud. Only empty air kept counsel now.

A hut crouched near the ring. Turf roof. Walls of stacked rock that had learned to stand together. Smoke wandered from a hole and lay down under the wind. Roblen rode in slow, then swung down and knocked. The door opened a crack. An eye like old amber studied from shadow.

“What word,” the voice asked. Not hostile. Not friendly. Tired of both.

“I seek road to the upper spring,” Roblen said. “And a thought from one who lives near the mountain.”

The door opened wider. An old woman faced him. Streaks of white hair escaped a kerchief and made their own wild border around a long face. Hands looked like roots, strong despite years.

“Spring gives what it is given,” she said. “Lately it gives a sore belly.”

“I have seen men pour from narrow casks into the bend,” Roblen said. “I have seen tracks where a good boot walked where river grass grows.”

“Good boots do bad work often enough,” she said. “A river is a road with no law but gravity. Anything poured farther up will find mouths farther down.”

“Have you seen smoke from the lair,” he asked. The word felt strange on the tongue. Like giving a shape to a thing he had not yet seen.

“Smoke comes one day and not another,” she said. “At times it smells of pine sap. At times it smells of something ill. I keep out of caves. I speak instead to the stones I have chosen to live with out here.” She tipped her head at the ring. “They mostly say what stones always say. Stand. Be cold. Remember.”

Roblen let his gaze drift to the mountain. The face of it bore a long scar where rock had slid, then stopped, then held. That scar drew the eye and made the rest of the mountain look like a body that had healed around a blade it could not push out.

“I will go up,” he said.

“You will,” she said. “Your kind always does. Take care where trees thin. Wind jumps there. A man can find himself a step shorter than his legs were made for. There is a ledge that carries through a cliff face. It looks too narrow to trust. It is wider than it looks. Do not look down while you test it. Look at the place where your foot wishes to be next.”

“Thank you,” Roblen said.

She peered past him at the mare. “Good bone,” she said. “Let her carry until the ledge. Tie her below. Go up alone. Caves do not want the company of horses.”

He nodded. “If you have clean water,” he added, “I will pay in work or coin.”

“Coin buys salt and not much else,” she said. “Bring me news if you return. Bring me none if you do not. There is a barrel behind the hut under a flat stone. Rain gathered there before the sky turned mean.”

Roblen filled his skin at the barrel and drank. Cold lay on the water like a truth that did not need a speech. He thanked the woman, tightened the girth, and rode toward the slope where pines thinned and rock took command.

Light went thin between trunks. Needles made a soft floor that took hoof and foot without complaint. The slope pitched. The mare breathed deep and even. A jay scolded from a branch without real faith in its own warning. Far above, a black shape lifted from a ledge and circled once. Eagle, by the long wings and the slow, confident turn. It watched and judged and decided no lesson could be taught today by a dive.

The ledge showed itself at last. A seam across a gray face. Snow clung to the lower edge like lace. Roblen tied the mare to a stub of root, rubbed her neck, and spoke into the ear.

“Stay,” he said. “I will be back before the light forgets me.”

He tested the ledge with a boot. Stone answered with a gritty whisper. He set weight, then shifted, then moved. One step. Two. The drop yawned without voice. He kept his eyes on the next hand hold, the next notch, the next patch of dry rock that would not lie about grip. Halfway across, wind leapt from the valley and slapped him flat to the face. Fingers locked. Jaw tightened until a tooth twinged. He waited until the gust spent itself and turned into a sigh that worked back up the mountain like regret. Then he moved again.

At the far end the ledge widened into a shelf. A wall of dark stone rose from that shelf with a mouth cut into it by fire and time. Not a gentle mouth. Teeth of basalt lined the lip. The air that came from within held a taste of old smoke and something else that pricked the nose like the smell in a smith’s yard when iron first flares in the coals.

Roblen stood very still and listened. No growl. No scrape. Only the slow, deep purr of heat that never fully sleeps. He looked down once, only once, to fix the route in his mind. The mare waited far below, a small brown shape patient as a stone that still breathes. A tiny thread of smoke from the hut drifted sideways and made a gray stitch through the air.

He stepped toward the mouth of the cave and let his eyes adjust to the dim. His hand did not rest on the hilt. A hand that rests without thought makes the blade think for the man. He wanted his mind first.

Inside, the floor sloped into a throat of rock. Char lines marked the ceiling in long arcs like the path of swallows. Black scabs of old soot clung to the higher stone. Far in, something caught the small light that bled from the mouth and gave it back with a weak, cold gleam. Not treasure. Not yet. Wet stone, and beyond that a suggestion of shape that might have been only shadow.

He drew one breath, slow and full. The air inside tasted like a long story told to itself. He let the breath go, then turned his head and listened again to the river that spoke in the world below. The two sounds made a braid. Water that wished to run. Fire that wished to rest. Somewhere between the two the truth would wait. He took another step, as careful as a man placing a word on the first line of a letter that must be written without mistake.

chapters.title: Broken Villages
chapters.content:
Broken Villages

Air cooled in a steady way as the tunnel drew him inward. Moisture beaded on stone, then slid down in small threads that joined, parted, and found new paths. A drip from high above struck a ledge and made a patient rhythm. Roblen stepped with care. The floor had a skin of soot near the mouth, then gave way to hard rock polished by seasons of heat and long rest. A pale dust lay in swirls, marked by prints larger than any beast of field. They set a stride he could measure only by breath, not by paces. Each mark showed a weight that had learned how to be gentle with stone.

Light thinned. He let the dark arrive rather than force a flame too soon. Eyes learned the gradient of shadow, and his feet learned the small tilt of the floor. When the mouth had become a memory behind him, he drew a coal from his pouch and cupped it with a twist of oiled cloth. A hush of spark took, and a small globe of dim light bloomed, no brighter than a winter moon behind cloud. He lifted it enough to read the walls.

Arcs of black ran along the vault. Not wild scars. Not the angry spray from a sudden burst. Lines had been laid there over years, in calm, in rest, in sleep. As if breath had washed the stone the way waves wash a shore when wind is quiet. Between those arcs, the rock showed a skin of mica, so that faint light came back in a scatter of pin stars. The place felt old without pride. It held its age the way a river holds its bed.

A side passage opened from the main throat and drew a thin wind that smelled of ice and high pine. He marked it and kept to the deeper way. The air around him warmed by a small degree. Not enough to ease the chill in mail. Enough to say the heart of the cave kept its own season. The drip above grew distant. Another sound replaced it. A long draw, then a pause, then a rumble that faded with a ground beat, like thunder set under earth.

He stopped and listened with his whole body. Breath shallow. Knees unlocked. Shoulder soft so that weight could move if it must. The sound came again. Long draw. Pause. Low rumble pushed through stone and settled in the belly. A sleeping thing, or a sick one. The old woman had said wind jumps on the ledge. Wind did not make that sound.

He moved again and let the glow lead, only a little. The tunnel broadened without warning into a chamber wide enough to hold a village green. Ceiling rose beyond the reach of the dim light and gave back a distant gleam like frost on a winter field under starlight. The floor sloped in a shallow bowl toward a bed of ash and charcoal that had been laid smooth by care and used without waste. Along one side, a black mirror of water lay still as a thought that wished to stay hidden. The faint skin on the surface caught his small light and made a weak shine that slid when a draft crossed.

Something vast lay beyond that bed, half in shadow, half in the mild reach of his coal. A ridge like a hill. A sweep of lines along the ground that had the order of ribs or the run of plate on a gate. A breath drew in. The shape lifted and spread by a few finger widths, then settled with a hollow sound that came from within, not from throat. He held his light steady and let the shape explain itself in pieces.

A head rose first. Not a lunge. A slow lift that told of weight and warning that belonged to the one who lifted it. Horns brushed the low outer line of the ceiling and left a pale scrape on soot. A narrow eye opened. Amber in the heart, ringed by clouded glass. The lid rose and fell once, then rose to half, as a man might open his eyes when fever will not let him sleep and will not let him wake. Nostrils flared. A breath came out through them with a whisper like water drawn through reeds.

Roblen did not reach for the hilt. Cold in the palm is a poor guide. He let the weight of the moment rest on his feet and trusted the bend of his knees more than the edge of his blade.

The head turned the length of a hand and fixed him. That small turn made scales run in a ripple over the neck. The scales had dulled, the way coins dull in damp cellars. Between plates the skin showed pale and dry. At the corners of the mouth, a crust had formed, faintly white, like salt dried where tears have been.

The dragon spoke. Not a roar. Not a growl. A word in the human tongue, formed with care and placed between them on the floor as if it were a cup of water one might share.

“Enough.”

The sound of that word reached more than the ear. It settled in the ribs. It touched the spine where old fears keep their small fires. It was not a threat. It was a request made by something that had learned its own strength long ago and no longer wished to spend it without need.

Roblen lowered the light a little. “I came to see,” he said. Simple words, plain and honest. He did not offer a name, nor ask for one. Names have weight, and the chamber had enough weight without more.

The dragon breathed in, and the rumble returned. When it spoke again, the voice had taken on a thread of dry humor that did not hide the effort behind it.

“Men always come to see,” it said. “They carry steel and hope the seeing needs the steel.” The head eased a small degree to the side. The eye studied the glow, then the hand that held it, then the boots that stood without tremble. “You have not set your hand to your blade. That is an old kindness.”

“I set my hand to what is needed,” Roblen said. He kept his voice even. “Much along the road has needed the hand open rather than closed.”

The head lifted enough to show the line of the throat. Scales there had cracked and lifted like old paint in sun. A cough rose and shook the massive chest in a deep rattle. Fire did not follow. Only a slow spill of smoke eased from the mouth and drifted low, thin and blue, before it vanished. The dragon turned toward the black water and moved two steps. The steps had a pain to them. Joints labored. A long hiss of breath escaped after the second.

The dragon reached the pool and drank. The tongue moved with a care that said each swallow cost something. When the mouth lifted, a slick skin clung and then tore. The dragon closed the eye for a moment and held still, as if letting the water find its place within a body that had forgotten the rightful shape of thirst.

Roblen knelt near the edge, far enough to show respect, close enough to read the water. The faint skin on the surface gathered at the touch of the tongue and then slid back into a flat that held a heavy shine under the small light. He dipped two fingers and rubbed them, then lifted to his nose. Coins again, and tar, and a bitter tang that lived at the back of the throat even without a swallow.

“The river in the valley tastes the same,” he said.

“The river brings what men give it,” the dragon answered. “It gives then to the fields, and the fields give to mouths, and mouths curse the sky for what the hands of men have poured. A circle with a cruel center.”

The words fell into the chamber and stirred something behind Roblen’s ribs that had not rested since the square. He set the small light on a shelf of stone and rose to stand without threatening height.

“Men say you foul the water,” he said.

“Men say many things,” the dragon said. The dry humor returned, thin as parchment. “It saves them from saying the few that matter.”

The head lowered toward the ash bed, then stilled halfway. The eye watched Roblen in a long, measured way that one uses when deciding if a bridge will hold. The lid lifted. The amber within caught a thread of the small light and warmed.

“Why are you here, man with the careful hands,” the dragon asked. “Do not say the king sent you. The mountain hears words set on drums and shouted from stages. Those words do not walk this far without losing their shape.”

Roblen let the question sit between them. Silence did its good work. Then he answered with the part of himself that had brought him over the ledge.

“I am here to find whether the talk in the square is truth or only noise,” he said. “I am here to learn if killing will cure or only feed hunger with a new story. I am here to carry back what I can carry back without shame when I set it down.”

The dragon listened with the stillness of a creature that knows how to hold a room with breath alone. The great chest rose and fell once. The tail, long as a city street, dragged a slow arc and left a smooth crescent in ash.

“You do not speak like the others,” it said. “You do not speak like a boy sent to win a crown’s smile. Your words smell of cold road and a small fire kept low for fear of strangers. Good. Fire kept low warms better.”

Roblen felt the set of his shoulders ease by a small degree. He did not smile. Smiles can be taken for promise. He pointed with a small tilt of the chin toward the pool.

“Why drink if it harms you,” he asked. “Snow lies on the ledges. Melt would serve better.”

The dragon gave a sound that might have been a laugh if it had not carried so much ache.

“Snow serves when a tongue can climb to it,” it said. “I have lain through a season of thin breath and weak wing. The stones beyond this chamber hold a wind that pushes me back like a door. I drink what the pool gives, and the pool gives what men carry from the valley. I have learned the taste of metals I do not name and resins I do not care to meet.”

The chamber seemed to draw nearer. Roblen moved to the pool and used the small bowl to lift a measure of the dark. He held it up and let the light show the skin as it gathered and broke. He poured it back slowly so that the surface did not slap. A ring formed where it spread, dull and stubborn. He wiped the bowl with his sleeve and returned it to the pouch.

“Your bed is laid with care,” he said. “The ceiling shows years of calm breath. This is a home kept, not a lair held for war.”

“War is something men drag with them,” the dragon said. “Beasts fight because flesh wishes to live. Men make a craft of it and sell the craft to one another. I have burned for my own life. I have not flown to burn a field I did not wish to eat.”

The head lowered to the ash and rested at last. The lids closed to a narrow line. A tremor ran along the flank, then eased. When the voice came again it held the softness of a fire banked to embers.

“You carry a name,” it said. “I will not take it without trade.”

“Roblen,” he said.

The lids lifted a little. The amber within warmed again. “Roblen,” the dragon said, shaping the word with care so that it came out whole. “I have had many names. The long one is for the old tongue and the old papers men keep in their deep places. Nacreban Iske Nordin. To those who wish less stone in the mouth, Nathan serves.”

The sound of Nathan in that chamber felt strange and right in the same breath. The small shape of it, the friendly plainness, set against the great length of body and the high vault of rock. Roblen gave a slow nod that let the name settle where it could live.

“Nathan,” he said. “I came to kill you if killing would cure. I do not see a cure in killing a creature who lies sick beside a poisoned pool.”

“Your eyes work,” Nathan said. The lids closed and opened in a patient blink. “Now you must carry what your eyes learned back down the mountain. That is the work that breaks men more than iron. The carrying of truth through rooms that have made a bed for a lie.”

Roblen looked past the bed of ash, deeper into the chamber. The small light reached a low wall where stones had been set in a line by a careful hand. Beyond that the floor dipped and rose. The shape beyond could have been only more rock. Or it could have been the edge of a place cut by tools rather than water. He did not step toward it. He kept his gaze there long enough to let Nathan see the question form.

“You keep watch on more than your own rest,” Roblen said.

“I keep watch on what the mountain keeps,” Nathan answered. “Sleep is light when one holds a door for those who have forgotten why it was built.”

Roblen did not press. Questions pushed too soon learn less than quiet hands. He returned to the pool and crouched. A thin thread of clean water touched his cheek where a drip from on high missed the skin of the pool and fell to stone. He caught it with two fingers and let it wet his tongue. Cold and true. The drip struck again and again, slow as a clock that had almost wound down.

“I can carry melt to you,” he said. “I can break the crust in the clefts and fill the skins. Not enough for strength, enough for one night of better breath.”

Nathan watched him without moving. The great sides rose once, fell once, with a long, slow sound that a man might make when he lets a pain leave by the door rather than the window.

“You would climb for a creature your king named a curse,” the dragon said.

“I would climb for what lives,” Roblen said. “That includes you. It includes a child with cracked lips at a well. It includes a miller who banks his fire rather than chase shadows with no names. All of that is work of the same kind.”

The dragon’s mouth shifted by the width of a finger. A ghost of a smile, there then gone.

“Bring melt,” Nathan said. “Bring it as a man brings a small flame into a cold room. It will not heat the stones. It will tell the room that heat remembers us.”

Roblen gathered his light, then the skins. He set his palm flat on the ash, not quite touching the scales, to show intent without presuming bond. The warmth from the bed eased the chill in his hand.

“Rest,” he said. “I will return before the dark climbs the ledge.”

He retraced his steps to the mouth, let the dim grow less dim, and found the seam of the ledge again. Wind had settled some. The jump it made earlier had turned to a steady push, the kind a man can lean into without losing his hat. He crossed with the same care, eyes fixed on the next hold, mind quiet. At the far end the mare lifted her head and blew a soft answer that said the world still held sense.

He climbed to the first drift of old snow and broke it with the heel of his hand. The crust cracked and gave a small music. Beneath it the snow lay clean and packed in blue layers. He filled the first skin, then the second, from the melt cupped in a shallow stone. He warmed each skin against his chest for a count of fifty breaths so that the chill would not bite the dragon’s tongue the way a lie bites trust.

On the way back across the ledge, a cloud dragged a wide sleeve over the sun and left the land below in a deeper shade. In that shade the river wound like a black thread through gray cloth. Thin smoke from the bend rose in a tired line. He thought of the men with narrow casks, and the care with which they had walked, and the way a boot tells on a man no matter how he places it.

Within the chamber, the air took him in again with that soft push of warmth. Nathan had not moved far. One forelimb now lay under the long jaw so that the head could rest without pulling at the cracked scales of the throat. The eye opened as Roblen came near. He held up the skins so that the light could climb them and show their intent.

He poured slowly into the bowl, then tilted the bowl to the dragon’s mouth. The tongue moved with grateful care. The water went in. The breath that followed came out with less rattle and more weight. He poured again. A third measure. The last, small and steady. When he set the empty skin aside, Nathan closed the eye and laid the head down all the way.

“Sleep,” Roblen said. “Let the melt tell your blood a better story.”

The lids did not lift. The chest rose and fell with a sound that shifted from a broken drum to a smoother bellows. He stood a long moment and let the quiet make its case. The small light burned low. He pinched it closed and let the chamber hold darkness again, comforted by the presence that filled it.

On the way back to the mouth, he stopped once more by the low wall. He did not cross it. He knelt and ran fingers along the nearest stones. They had been placed, not rolled there by chance. The top faces had been worn by hands, not by water. On one edge, a shallow cut marked a symbol that did not belong to wind or claw. A wedge set between two lines that met at a point. He had seen the shape once in a book kept by a priest who loved old stories more than sermons. It had named a pact in a tongue that needed patience to read.

He breathed out. The sound moved over the stones and made a small echo that came back like a whisper from another room. He stood, gathered the skins, and found his way into the winter afternoon.

Clouds had opened again and let through a light that looked tired but honest. The mare stamped and watched him with that wide regard horses carry for men who go into holes and come out of them changed in ways horses do not wish to guess. He rubbed her neck and set his forehead to the warm place between her eyes.

“Good work,” he said. “Good patience.”

The wind carried the thin smell of smoke from the hut below. He thought of the old woman and her steady gaze. He thought of Serenya and her calm voice that carried the shape of truth without needing to shout. He thought of Garran and the bend and the way men choose to live while they wait for help that does not come.

He looked back at the mouth and made a quiet promise that did not require the mountain to hear it. He would melt again. He would carry more than melt once he knew what the stones beyond the wall were keeping. He would bring down what a square had asked for, though it might not be the sort of trophy a king would hang in a hall.

He took up the reins and led the mare along the path to the shelf where the ledge began. The shadow of the mountain reached over him and moved with him like a cloak. Far below, the river curved, dark and stubborn, toward fields that waited to be told a better story. He set his foot to the first hold and stepped into that story with care.

chapters.title: The Dragon’s Lair
chapters.content:
The Dragon’s Lair

Light broke over the ridge slow and thin, and the mountain took it without hurry. Roblen led the mare along the narrow shelf where the pines left off and the scrub began. He spoke to her in the simple way of men who have more to do than words can cover. The air held a bite that did not care for brave faces. His hands remembered the warmth of the small fire from the night, then forgot it as stone and wind pressed close.

At the ledge he tied the reins to the same twisted root and checked the knot with a pull. A breath to steady mind and muscle. Then the span across the gray face, foot by careful foot, palm to the rock where the grain could be trusted. Ravens drifted in slow circles over the lower bowl. Their voices sounded like old ropes that still hold.

The mouth of the cave gave him that steady warmth again. A house that had no love for him and yet accepted him because he came with a purpose that did not pretend to be something else. He moved through the first throat of stone with the same dim coal, kept small so that shadow could hold its own and outline what mattered. The bed of ash came into view. The black mirror of water lay still. A curl of smoke hung near the roof like a remembered thought.

Nathan lifted his head when Roblen came close. The eye opened with effort, then steadied. A breath drew long and shook a little at the end. Roblen held up the skins and then the bowl, small as a prayer in a cathedral. He poured with care. The tongue moved, the throat worked in a slow pull that did not scrape so much as it had the night before. When the last measure slipped down, a quiet filled the space that was more than the absence of sound. It felt like the way a ground settles after a tremor and makes peace with itself again.

“Thank you,” Nathan said. The word carried the ring of a tool set down on a bench after good work. Not light, not heavy, right.

Roblen set the skins aside to dry on a stone. “There is more where snow lies in shadow,” he said. “I can carry until shoulder fails. It will not be enough on its own. It will be more than nothing.”

Nathan watched him. The lid rose and fell once. “Men come with steel and leave with stories,” he said. “You carry water and leave the story where it belongs. This suits me.”

Roblen glanced toward the low wall beyond the bed. The stones there had not been set by the hand of chance. He knelt and studied the top line. Scratches crossed its face. Not the aimless scratches of animals. Marks that remembered a set of rules. He did not cross yet. He turned back.

“I found a cut on one stone,” he said. “A wedge set between lines that met. I have seen the sign before in a place that loved old things. It named an oath.”

“It named the bond that held this valley when men still listened,” Nathan said. His voice thinned a little and then steadied. “Come. I will show what the mountain keeps.”

Roblen rose and stepped to the edge of the low wall. Nathan did not rise. The massive body barely moved. Yet a presence filled the space as if the chamber itself stood to attend what would be shown. Roblen placed a palm on the top stone as a man places a hand on a door before he enters a room of sleep. Then he crossed.

Beyond the wall the floor dipped into a shallow basin. The rock there shone with that mica skin that catches stray light and makes stars where none have any right to be. At the far side the basin rose to a platform of smooth slate. Upon that, a slab of black stone rested on two uprights, each marked from base to top with rows of small, patient cuts. The cuts had been made by a hand that knew patience the way a river knows distance.

Roblen lifted the coal a little. The small light walked those cuts and woke a scatter of meanings. Lines made figures. Figures made scenes. A river drawn as a bend of silver line with small marks for fish and reeds. A mountain cut in simple triangles. A form that could only be a dragon, shown not as a thing of fire eating villages, but as a long shape coiled around a circle of stones. The circle itself carved with the wedge and the meeting lines that named a pact. He leaned closer and let the story unfold along the slab.

At the top row a king stood with a crown that was simply made, more band than glory. He held no sword. His hand reached toward a long shape seated in profile, and between that hand and that shape a small disc had been carved with care. A heart. Not large, not torn, a circle with a single line that ran through and continued into the chest of the other. The next row showed rain falling clean on fields while the circle rested between man and beast. Wheat heads on simple stalks rose in neat lines. Children played near a river that wound true.

Lower rows darkened. Men in cloaks held narrow casks. They leaned and poured into the river while their faces looked at each other and not at what their hands did. The fish turned on their sides and were carried away. The clean line over the fields broke. Wheat bent and failed. Under that, the circle that had once run from chest to chest now lay broken on the ground between. The king shown there wore more metal and less sense. His hand did not reach. His hand closed around the hilt of a blade.

Roblen stood quiet a long time. The story did not need his voice. It needed breath long enough to live in mind and marrow. He let it live there and burned it in like a mark that would not wash out. At last he spoke, low and even, to the stone, to his own hands, to the air that moved slow in the chamber.

“They broke the bond,” he said. “They blamed you while men poured night into the river.”

“Truth does not need a witness to be true,” Nathan said. “It goes on when men sleep. It wakes when they wake. Sometimes it waits in stone until a palm warms the cut and remembers why the cut was made.”

Roblen ran a thumb along the upper row again. His nail found the small groove where the line that marked the heart continued from one figure to the other. It had been cut deeper than the rest. The hand that made it had wanted that detail to remain when other marks wore thin.

“How did a man share life with you,” he asked. He kept the words slow. A quick tongue dishonors the cut that made such marks.

Nathan breathed in. The sound did not scrape as much this time, yet it climbed the wall and hung there like a banner.

“The lore says this,” Nathan said. “A ruler placed his hand upon a stone at a doorway, and a guardian placed a talon upon the same, and the keepers of the vault spoke old words that carry weight. A binding began as a careful fire begins. Not a blaze. A coal set from one hearth to another. Half life, half strength, shared willingly. From that sharing the land took its cue. Creature and crown breathed to a single rhythm and made a season where plenty did not shame the poor and strength did not make a sport of weakness.”

Roblen looked at his palms. Lines there made their own cuts. Small, white, healed, from years of wood and steel and rope. He turned his hand and set the pad to the stone. It felt cold and rough and true.

“No keepers stand here now,” he said. “There is only a man with a task, and a creature who lives, and a room of stone that remembers more than people bother to read.”

“Keepers leave tools behind when they die,” Nathan said. “Words. Marks. A pattern of stones that fit only one way. A thing built into the rock that answers a hand if the hand intends what the thing was made to serve.” The dragon shifted just enough to ease a joint. The movement made a soft grind in the ash. “You felt the cut with your thumb,” he added. “Some part of you knew where that line should go next.”

Roblen let out a breath he had not noticed he held. He stood at the platform and traced the air above the disc that named a heart. In his mind he set the line again between figures. A warmth rose behind the sternum and spread to the shoulder, not strong, not weak, insistent and clean.

“I cannot command a crown,” he said. “I cannot open a granary or raise an army with a gesture. I can choose where my own life goes next.”

“That choice is larger than the crown knows,” Nathan said. “A man can set a pattern with one act and that pattern can pull other acts after it like boats along a rope. I have watched men do harm in this way and call it order. Once in a line of seasons a man will do the other thing and the rope will pull toward light.”

Roblen lifted the coal. The small flame caught a fleck of mica and woke it. The light ran along the flecks like a message passed from hand to hand. The slab on its uprights looked less like a tomb and more like a table laid for a true talk.

“What must be said to wake the bond,” he asked.

“Not grand words,” Nathan said. “Grand words break when weight sits on them. Simple words hold. A promise given with both hands on the stone. A naming of what will be shared and what will be kept. A clear ask. A clean answer. The mountain hears the shape of such things even when the sound itself dies.”

Roblen set his palm flat on the slab. Stone cooled his skin. He placed the other hand upon his chest and felt the beat that had been with him since he first woke to a world that did not forgive or favor any more than it must. He closed his eyes and looked inward with the same patience he used when watching a trail for signs that did not wish to be read.

“I can say the words,” he said. “Can I mean them. I do not know if I will live long after. I do not know if the crown will call for my head. I do not know if men with narrow casks will set the river right when a dragon rises whole.”

“You know what kind of man you wish to be when you sleep,” Nathan said. “That is the only sort that matters when the last light of a day leaves your room.” A pause, then a lift of humor, dry and kind. “Besides, a dragon with strength can teach men with narrow casks to find another trade.”

Roblen smiled without showing teeth. The slab held his hand steady. The chamber held his doubt and did not judge it. He spoke, not loud, not soft, the way he had spoken to the child at the well when he split the bread.

“I offer half my heart’s life,” he said. “I offer willingly. I ask that the bond heal what men have harmed. I ask that breath return to a creature who guards what was set here to keep us honest. I ask that the land hear and answer in its own time. I will carry the cost without complaint.”

Stone under his palm went warm. Not hot, not child of flame. Warm as a hearth that has been banked all night and comes back to itself when a hand stirs the ash. The warmth climbed his arm and touched the place where his own heart kept time. For a moment the beat stuttered. Then it found a new measure. Not faster, not slower. In concert. Another rhythm joined it, low and deep, like a drum that calls a village in the evening.

Nathan drew a breath that reached all the way to the high roof. The sound began ragged, then ran smooth, then settled into a strong pull. Scales along the throat eased. A crust at the mouth softened and broke clean. The eye opened clear. Amber burned bright at the core and shed the cloud that had sat there since sickness set in.

Roblen swayed with the change. The world tilted, then steadied. He lifted his hand from the slab and looked at the palm. A faint line, no wider than a hair, crossed the skin where the wedge mark had pointed. It did not bleed. It did not hurt. It looked like the first cut a carver makes when he begins a careful work.

Nathan rose. The full height of him filled the chamber. Wings unfurled by a hand’s width, then folded, then unfurled again, as if memory returned to muscle in small wakeful waves. His head came down close and the eye met Roblen at a level where equals speak and call each other by chosen names.

“Roblen,” Nathan said. “The bond holds. The stone heard. So did I.” The voice ran smooth now, with a depth that sat right in the chest when a man listened. “You have given much. I will give more in return. The river will not forgive in a day. We will make the men who wronged it find their own faces again.”

Roblen took a breath of the cave’s warmer air and let it out in a long line. He felt older in a way that had nothing to do with years and everything to do with choice. He stood straighter without deciding to. He looked at the slab again, then at the basin with its mica stars, then at the path back to the bed of ash where the dragon had lain like a hill in winter.

“We will need proof,” he said. “Stone that speaks in lines a farmer can read while he holds a bowl and decides whether to give you bread or throw a stone. We will need to show where the river was fouled. We will need to take away the tools that make it easy to do harm.”

Nathan turned his head toward the dark beyond the platform. “There is more there,” he said. “The vault carries records that do not rot. Names. Places. Marks of casks and makers of pitch. Men think the mountain keeps only secrets. It keeps accounts.”

Roblen felt a fierce, quiet joy rise in him, clean and sharp as the air that pours through a door when a blizzard breaks and the sky shows blue. He banked the feeling and shaped it into purpose.

“Then we will open that door,” he said. “We will carry what lies within down the ledge and past the old woman’s ring and along the river. We will speak names in squares where drums beat. We will let the people weigh what they hear.”

He looked toward the mouth of the cave, where the light had shifted from harsh to honest as the day walked past noon. A thin sound came from far down the slope, not loud, not close. A horn. One long note. Then a second, short. A call he knew from the city. Patrol on the move. Riders checking hillsides for smoke that does not come from hearths.

Nathan heard it as well. The ear fin lifted, then settled.

“Visitors,” the dragon said. The tone held neither fear nor surprise. Only the kind of readiness that lives in creatures who have learned that peace, when it comes, must be defended with the same patience that earned it.

“Not yet,” Roblen said. “Patrols keep to the lower ridge at this hour. They watch the river. They tell themselves they guard the crown and they do, though the crown has forgotten what true guard means.”

He returned to the slab and pressed his palm once more to the warm stone, as a man touches a friend’s shoulder before leaving a room to do a hard thing. Then he crossed back over the low wall to the ash bed. Nathan lowered his head so that Roblen could lay a hand near the hinge of the jaw, where scale gives way to a softer skin. The contact felt right. Not a pledge spoken. A pledge kept.

“I will bring more melt,” Roblen said. “And I will bring a pair of hands from the valley who can read and carry and speak without fear. Not a herald. Someone who knows how to fix a wheel and mend a fence and count sacks. Truth has a better voice when a neighbor speaks it.”

“Bring Serenya,” Nathan said, as if he had known her name all along. “Healers hear what men do not say. Healers make other men listen.”

Roblen blinked once. Surprise came and went. The dragon had lived through more seasons than any number written on paper. A sick valley would not hide its talk from such ears.

“I will bring her,” he said.

He gathered the empty skins and the small coal. The light dimmed to a red bead that still held heat. At the mouth of the cave he looked back. Nathan stood in the old bed, no longer a hill of winter, no longer only a patient weight. The eye shone. Breath moved like a tide. A faint curl of smoke rose and carried the smell of pine, not pitch.

“Rest,” Roblen said.

“Return,” Nathan answered.

The ledge felt different underfoot on the way out. Not wider. Not safer. True. Wind met him and did not try to push him from the face. He crossed, reached the shelf, and found the mare with head high and ears forward. He stroked her neck and felt the life there answer his hand in the steady rhythm he had always trusted.

Down the slope, the ring of stones held its own quiet. Smoke from the hut rose straight for a moment and then bent under a high current. The horn sounded again from the lower ridge and fell away. Roblen swung into the saddle and turned toward the path that would take him by the old woman, past the quarry, along the bend, and back to a door marked with a healer’s hand.

The valley waited. The river carried both harm and hope. Truth had a place to stand now. He would build a floor under it and make sure it did not fall when men began to shout.

chapters.title: The Hidden Vault
chapters.content:
The Hidden Vault

Dawn waited behind a thin veil, then stepped through with slow feet. Frost glazed the grass below the pines and caught the light in small, stubborn sparks. Roblen took the slope steady, one hand on the mare’s withers for the tight turns, mind set on the path back to the ring of stones. Crows moved from tree to tree with patient hops. Each call sounded like a question that knew its own answer.

Smoke from the hut drew a straight seam into the sky before the wind found it and bent it east. The old woman stood by the door with a bowl of oats and a wooden spoon. Steam rose and made a pale cloud over her hands. She watched without surprise as horse and rider came out of the trees.

“Your step changed,” she said. The spoon tapped once on the rim. “A man comes down a mountain different from the one who went up if the mountain meant to keep him.”

“The mountain kept me,” Roblen said. “And gave me back with work to do.”

She set the bowl on a flat rock. “Eat while you tell it,” she said. “Work listens better when the belly agrees to sit for a while.”

The first spoonful carried plain comfort. Oats, a little salt, a clean taste that did not try to be more than it was. He lifted his head and spoke so the wind would carry only as far as the ring.

“The river is fouled by men,” he said. “The lair holds a pool that tastes the same. The creature lives. Ill, not wicked. There is a vault beyond his bed. Carved records. A pact cut in stone.”

Her eyes narrowed, not in doubt, in care. “The old bond,” she said. “My mother said her mother spoke of it when nights ran long. A king who shared his heart and a valley that remembered. Then men with short memories built barrels and forgot how to listen.”

“The seal marks cut deep,” Roblen said. “Names sit there waiting. Marks of cask makers. Signs of roads used after dark. Truth enough to fit in both hands.”

She tipped her chin toward the slope. “You will carry those hands into rooms where men do not care for truth,” she said. “Carry anyway. Come back if you bleed. I keep linen and hot water. I keep a mouth that does not gossip.”

He thanked her and swung up. The mare took the narrow path with a quick, eager step, as if the chill had become a game she meant to win. At the first opening in the trees he looked across the bowl of the valley. The river ran black silk under the dull sun. Thin pillars of smoke marked the bend and two other hamlets that clung to the banks like barnacles on an old hull. Far off, a rider line moved along a ridge. Banners hung limp. The horns from the evening had left no patrol at the ledge. Luck does its work when courage cannot.

By the time the quarry rose on his right, the day had found its color. Not bright. Honest. Rock faces showed vein and scar. The abandoned wheel leaned where it always had, yet the angle looked new. The river below played at a series of steps and sent up a voice that rang off the stone like a choir of careful hammers.

Garran stood near the skiff with sleeves rolled and hands red from cold water. A scrape of flint on board made a dry rasp. Two boys tugged at a net and scolded each other with the seriousness of men twice their age. The men looked up when hooves clicked on slate.

“You come back,” Garran said. “That puts you ahead of most who go seeking answers.”

“Answers do not enjoy being hunted,” Roblen said. “They prefer to be coaxed.” He slid from the saddle and tied the mare to a hitch post someone had set there years ago for the same purpose. “There were men on the bend at night. I will need more than talk. Anything caught under the roots after the last high water.”

Garran grunted and wiped both hands on his coat. “A boy pulled a narrow cask out from under a willow this morning,” he said. “Heavy with silt. He wanted to make a drum of it. The mother said better to burn what you do not understand. I told her to wait. It sits by the shed.”

They walked over the beaten grass to a low lean to that let the wind run by without stealing the roof. A narrow barrel leaned on its side against the wall. Staves tight. Hoops set from a smith with a steady eye. Pitch seeped along one seam and dried there like black wax. Roblen crouched and brushed silt from the belly with a bit of net float. A stamp came up through the grime. A tiny star above a pair of crossed reeds. He cleaned more. Letters followed in a hand used to good trade. A place name. A maker. The stamp cut the wood after the pitch set, which said the cooper had no pride to keep.

“Reedhouse,” Garran read. He spat to one side in a way that did not aim at a man but did not hide what the mouth felt. “We sell fish on that dock when the river behaves. They pay in small coin and take a share for the right to stand on their planks.”

Roblen turned the cask so the seam faced the light. The pitch had been mixed with a resin that left a thin green sheen where it caught the sun. He touched a fingertip to the line and smelled it. Coins again. Then a pine bite that came sour.

“Do not burn this,” Roblen said. “We will carry it to the city. With this, and with the marks in the vault, people will have more than a shouted story.”

“You can drag truth across a square and some will still step around it,” Garran said. The words came flat, not unkind. “But a cooper’s mark makes a man sweat when you ask questions with that in your hands.”

“Where do the night boats cut in,” Roblen asked.

Garran tilted his head toward the bend. “There,” he said. “Under the low limb. A skiff with three men can slide in and let the current hide the sound. We keep a fire, but a stick will die if you do not feed it. Men choose the moment.”

Roblen took a slow breath and let it go. The wind lifted a thread of his hair and let it fall again. “I need a cart,” he said. “I need a man who knows every yard between this bend and the south gate. The cart will carry the cask. I will carry the rest.”

“I will walk beside you,” Garran said. “My boys will hold the nets and keep the gossip home. If soldiers ask why a fisher talks to a knight, I will say the knight asked the way to a deep pool and I showed him a shallow one. Men like that sort of joke.”

They set the barrel on its end and rolled it to the green. Wood thumped in a rhythm that drew eyes to doorways. No one called out. Lines tightened around mouths and stayed that way. Roblen thanked Garran, mounted, and took the road toward the city at a trot, mind already on a door with a painted mark and a woman with steady hands.

By mid afternoon the lower ward opened its crooked arms. The streets gave back the hoofbeats in a hollow roll that made houses sound like empty chests. Children hopped along a chalk grid scratched on the cobbles, feet careful, eyes not quite on the game. A boy dropped a stone when he saw the narrow cask lashed on Garran’s small cart. The stone hit the chalk square and broke there with a click.

Serenya’s door stood as before, the symbol above it white and true. He knocked. The door opened with a soft hinge sound that said oil had done its quiet work. She held a cloth in one hand and a pestle in the other. A bowl of crushed thyme sat on the table. The room wore the same scent as the first day. Clean wood. Herb. Water warmed to hold a wash.

“You came back with wind in your face and a plan in your eyes,” Serenya said. She set the pestle down and looked over his shoulder to the lane. The cask drew a small line between her brows that was not worry, not yet. “Come in.”

He stepped into the warmth and spoke while she gathered the kettle and laid fresh cups on the table. “The dragon is named Nathan,” he said. “Sick, not wicked. The pool at his bed tastes like the bend. There is a vault with cuts that carry the old oath. Men with narrow casks have poured poison into the river by night.”
